problems.title: Binary Search
problems.tagline: Given a sorted array and a target, return the target's index, or -1 if absent. O(log N).
statement: Binary search halves the search space each iteration by comparing the middle element to the target. Simple in principle, notoriously easy to get wrong — off-by-one errors, integer overflow on `(lo + hi) / 2`, infinite loops when the halving misses a case.
Read the array on line 1 (space-separated), the target on line 2. Output the index (0-based), or -1.
The classic gotcha: `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` overflows for large arrays. Prefer `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`. Small in Java/C where int is 32-bit; irrelevant in Python (arbitrary precision).
constraints: Array is sorted in ascending order.

solutions.python:
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
target = int(input())
lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
ans = -1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if nums[mid] == target: ans = mid; break
    elif nums[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1
print(ans)

problems.title: Fibonacci
problems.tagline: Read N and print the Nth Fibonacci number. F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, F(N) = F(N-1) + F(N-2).
statement: The Fibonacci sequence: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ... — each number is the sum of the previous two.
Three canonical approaches, in increasing sophistication:
Recursion (bad — O(2^N)) demonstrates the definition literally.
Iteration (good — O(N) time, O(1) memory) is the pragmatic solution.
Matrix exponentiation (O(log N)) is what you use if N is really big.

solutions.python:
n = int(input())
a, b = 0, 1
for _ in range(n):
    a, b = b, a + b
print(a)

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
problems.tagline: Given two sorted arrays, print a single merged sorted output.
statement: Two sorted inputs, one sorted output. The two-pointer walk runs in O(n + m) — advance the pointer whose current element is smaller, emit it, repeat. When one array runs out, drain the other.
This is the merge step of merge sort and one of the most fundamental array operations. Every sort-adjacent algorithm eventually calls something like it.
Read array A on line 1, array B on line 2. Print merged on line 3.
constraints: Both arrays are sorted in ascending order.

solutions.python:
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
b = list(map(int, input().split()))
i = j = 0
out = []
while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
    if a[i] <= b[j]: out.append(a[i]); i += 1
    else:            out.append(b[j]); j += 1
out.extend(a[i:]); out.extend(b[j:])
print(*out)

problems.title: Palindrome Check
problems.tagline: Read a string, print "true" if it is a palindrome (case-insensitive, alphanumerics only), else "false".
statement: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. Real-world variants strip whitespace and punctuation and lowercase everything first — "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" is a palindrome by that definition.
Standard O(n) approach: filter and lowercase the string, then two-pointer compare from ends inward. Alternative: reverse and compare — same complexity, simpler code, slightly more allocation.

examples.input: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

examples.explanation: The empty string is trivially a palindrome.

solutions.python:
s = ''.join(c.lower() for c in input() if c.isalnum())
print('true' if s == s[::-1] else 'false')

tests.stdin: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

problems.title: Reverse a Linked List
problems.tagline: Reverse a singly linked list. Iterative (O(1) extra space) or recursive (O(n) stack).
statement: You are given the head of a singly-linked list. Reverse it and print the new head-to-tail sequence.
The iterative solution uses three pointers — prev, curr, next — and walks the list once, rewriting each `curr.next` to point at prev. O(n) time, O(1) space.
The recursive solution is short but uses O(n) stack; recurse to the end, then unwind rewriting pointers.
For this challenge, take the list as space-separated integers on line 1 and print the reversed sequence.

solutions.python:
# Iterative reversal — no actual linked list needed for this I/O shape;
# the algorithm shape is preserved: walk once, rebuild in reverse.
vals = input().split()
print(*vals[::-1])

problems.title: Reverse String
problems.tagline: Reverse the input string. In-place is preferred where the language allows.
statement: Read a single line from standard input and print it reversed.

The archetype "hello, world" of algorithm interviews — every language has a one-liner reversal, and the value of practising it is seeing how each language expresses the same idea. C++ has `reverse(s.begin(), s.end())`. Python has `s[::-1]`. Java has `new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()`. In assembly you write a loop.

examples.explanation: A palindrome reads the same reversed.

constraints: ASCII input only — multi-byte UTF-8 handling is out of scope for the base problem.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.tagline: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
statement: You are given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`. Return the indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`.
You may assume that each input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. You can return the answer in any order.

The naive O(n²) approach is a double loop. The optimal O(n) approach is a single pass with a hash map that stores each value's index as you scan — for every new value `v`, check whether `target - v` is already in the map; if it is, you have your pair.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.tagline: Given two strings, print "true" if one is a permutation of the other.
statement: An anagram is a rearrangement of a string's characters. `listen` ↔ `silent`. `evil` ↔ `vile`. Not: `hello` ↔ `world`.

Two canonical approaches: (a) sort both strings and compare — O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space; (b) count characters in a hashmap or frequency array and compare — O(n) time, O(k) space where k is the alphabet size. For ASCII, k = 128, so (b) is strictly better.
Read two lines. Print "true" or "false".

solutions.python:
from collections import Counter
a = input(); b = input()
print('true' if Counter(a) == Counter(b) else 'false')

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.tagline: Given a string containing only (){}[], determine whether every opener has its matching closer, correctly nested.
statement: A valid bracket string satisfies: every opener has a matching closer of the same kind, and openers close in reverse order of appearance ((()) is valid; ([)] is not).
The canonical solution is a stack: push openers, on a closer pop and compare. If the stack ends non-empty or a pop mismatches, the string is invalid.
Prints `true` or `false`.
